title: The Bias Blind Spot
objective: After this level you can explain why people spot bias in others far more easily than in themselves.
summary: People see bias in others far more readily than in themselves, because they judge themselves by their thoughts and others by their behavior. Intelligence doesn't shrink the blind spot.

cards.headline: Quick: are you more biased or less biased than the average person?
cards.body: If you said "less", you're in large company. In surveys, people rate themselves as less subject to biases than the average American. They can't all be right. This level is about why the answer feels so obvious from the inside.

cards.fact: People see bias far more readily in others than in themselves.
cards.context: Psychologists Emily Pronin, Daniel Lin and Lee Ross called this the bias blind spot in a 2002 paper. Notice the twist. Every trap in this chapter so far, you can probably spot in a friend. Spotting it in yourself is the hard part.

cards.headline: Why you can't see it
cards.body: When you judge yourself, you look inward, at your thoughts and intentions, and they seem fair. But bias often works outside awareness, so looking inward finds nothing. When you judge others, you look at what they actually do. There's a second reason: your own view feels like a plain view of reality, so people who see things differently seem to be the biased ones.

cards.headline: Smarter isn't safer
cards.body: You might hope intelligence helps. In a 2012 study, Richard West, Russell Meserve and Keith Stanovich found that higher cognitive ability did not shrink the blind spot; if anything, it went with a larger one. What did help, in a 2007 study, was learning how much of judgment runs outside awareness. The habit: judge yourself by your behavior, the way you'd judge anyone else.

cards.headline: Blind spot: found
learned: People see bias in others more than in themselves
We judge ourselves by thoughts, others by actions
Intelligence doesn't shrink the blind spot
Judge yourself by your behavior too
